newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - API inventory data brings no surprises.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - API inventory data brings no surprises.

text.p: This week's inventory report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) surprised no one, fulfilling oil market expectations that the data would weigh in as neutral, traders and analysts said.
They noted the build in crude stocks and the drop in refinery utilization rates was a textbook case of what happens when refiners are in the middle of winter maintenance.
"These numbers are really in line with expectations, and the crude build is clearly showing turnarounds," said Gerald Samuels, managing director at ARB Oil.
Still, some said the 3.73 million barrel build in crude stocks was a bit more voluminous than expected, which could add bearish pressure to a market that has been moving lower.
"This report shouldn't have any impact, but the market is bearish overall, so ultimately it may be considered bearish," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst at Cargill Investor Services.
Blakeslee noted that the lack of concern surrounding historically-low total crude stocks of 289.8 million barrels shows how much the market is now comfortable with low stocks.
"We're in a new age," Blakeslee said, noting the 300 million barrel level a year ago triggered bullish responses.
On the refined products front, gasoline stocks rose by 1.84 million barrels to 201.3 million, helped by imports that rose by 84,000 barrels from week-ago levels to 329,000 barrels per day, API said.

Sources said the gasoline numbers did not contribute bearishness to the market outlook, since winter refinery maintenance is now in full swing and stocks need to rise in the coming ahead of the seasonal surge in gasoline stocks.
Refinery utilization rates moved down another 0.8 of a percentage point last week to 89.1 percent, remaining under the psychologically important 90 percent threshold.
On the the distillate front, stocks meanwhile fell by 2.85 million barrels to 119.6 million, just 626,000 barrels below year-ago levels.

That drop included a 1.65 million barrel drop in heating oil stocks, and a 1.2 million barrel drop in low sulphur diesel stocks. The heating oil draw itself included a 2.04 million barrel drop in the Northeast, the world's biggest home heating oil market.
Initial reactions to the data on ACCESS were mixed, heading higher after first moving downward.
